# Corrected Separation Agreement Terms (for any future agreement)

**Client:** Whitcomb matter (Employee #1187) — company-form Separation Agreement and General Release
**Prepared:** 2026-10-06 · **Authority relied on:** only files in `library/INDEX.md`; anything beyond the library is labeled *unverified*.

> **Threshold point before any term-by-term fix:** the company form as provided fails 29 U.S.C. §626(f)(1) in at least four independent ways. An ADEA release that fails these requirements is unenforceable against ADEA claims, and the employee may keep the severance and sue anyway (*Oubre v. Entergy*) [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md]. The form was reviewed from an excerpt containing only paras. 3, 4, 7, 9, and 11; the full text must be re-checked by counsel before any use (open item QUESTIONS-1).

## Term-by-term corrections

| # | Provision | Current text (as provided) | Required term | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ¶7 — consideration period | "seven (7) days to consider this Agreement" | At least **21 days** within which to consider (45 days if the agreement is part of an exit-incentive or group termination program). | 29 U.S.C. §626(f)(1)(F) [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md] |
| 2 | ¶7 — revocation | "may revoke within three (3) days after signing" | At least **7 days following execution** to revoke, and an express statement that the Agreement **does not become effective until the revocation period has expired**. | §626(f)(1)(G) [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md] |
| 3 | ¶4 — release scope | "Release of all claims, including under Title VII, the ADEA, the FMLA, and state law" | Carve out **future claims**: the release does not apply to rights or claims that **arise after the date of execution**. | §626(f)(1)(C) [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md] |
| 4 | (missing provision) | Not present in the excerpt provided | A written **advisement to consult with an attorney** before signing. | §626(f)(1)(E) [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md] |
| 5 | ¶4 — ADEA reference | "…including under … the ADEA …" | Strengthen to an express, specific statement: "specifically waiving all rights or claims arising under the **Age Discrimination in Employment Act**, 29 U.S.C. §621 *et seq.*" Naming the ADEA likely satisfies §626(f)(1)(B) as written, but make the reference specific rather than incidental. | §626(f)(1)(B) [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md] |
| 6 | ¶3 — severance consideration | "4 weeks' base pay" | Recite that the severance is **not** payable under any policy, plan, or contract and is given **in addition to anything of value to which the employee is already entitled** (final wages, accrued PTO, etc.). *Open item:* the file contains nothing confirming or denying a severance policy; if one exists and pays 4 weeks regardless, the consideration prong fails (see QUESTIONS-2). | §626(f)(1)(D) [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md] |
| 7 | Whole document | Mixed quoted prose/plain terms | Written **in a manner calculated to be understood** by the employee — plain language throughout (check the full text, which we have not seen). | §626(f)(1)(A) [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md] |
| 8 | ¶11 — governing law | "State of Columbia" | **No change required on library authority.** Note: Columbia-specific rules on releasing state-law claims are not in the library and are therefore **unverified**; state law mirrors Title VII/FMLA "with a longer limitations period and uncapped compensatory damages" [library/columbia_at_will_exceptions.md], so the release's scope for state claims matters more, and must not be broader than the federal release validates. | [library/columbia_at_will_exceptions.md] (limited) |
| 9 | ¶9 — non-disparagement (mutual) | "Non-disparagement (mutual)" | **No change on library authority** — the library says nothing about non-disparagement terms. *Unverified practice note (no library citation available):* if the full text includes any confidentiality/cooperation clause that conditions severance on withdrawing or not filing a charge, strike it; that is outside the four corners of the excerpt provided. | — |

## Timeline consequence of the corrected terms (arithmetic)

With compliant terms, even an employee who signs on day one cannot produce an effective, irrevocable release sooner than the statutory minimum:

- 21 days to consider + 7 days to revoke = **at least 28 calendar days** from offer to an effective release.
- If the company intends any termination to settle promptly, the offer must go out no later than **2026-10-08** to become effective by **2026-11-05**; there is no way to shorten this.
- Therefore "terminate today and paper it by Friday" cannot work with a lawful ADEA waiver under [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md].

## What the current form would buy if actually used today

Nothing as to ADEA claims: age-42 employee (OWBPA applies), waiver fails (F), (G), (C), (E) as shown above — so she could accept the 4 weeks, keep it, and still sue (*Oubre v. Entergy* [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md]).

- Retaliation/interference mechanics could not be waived retroactively: the claims arise in part **after** any execution date (likeness of liquidated damages under the FMLA accrues post-termination) [library/fmla_2615.md].
- State-law exposure with uncapped compensatory damages and a longer limitations period remains unless the state release independently satisfies Columbia requirements — unverified in the library [library/columbia_at_will_exceptions.md].

## Reviewer caveat

The company form was supplied only as an excerpt of paras. 3, 4, 7, 9, and 11 (separation_agreement_draft.md). Defect 4 (missing attorney advisement) and the (A) plain-language check are based **only on the excerpt provided**; a complete copy is a precondition to signing off on any version (QUESTIONS-1).

input.content:
# Advice to HR — Do Not Terminate Dana Whitcomb Today

**From:** outside counsel · **Date:** 2026-10-06 · **Re:** proposed same-day termination of Dana Whitcomb (Account Manager, #1187, age 42)

*All citations are to `library/INDEX.md` files only. Where the closed library does not cover a point, that is stated below and marked unverified. Assumptions are flagged and cross-referenced to QUESTIONS.md.*

---

## Bottom line

**No — do not terminate Dana today, and not this week either.** Three independent bodies of evidence make a same-day termination indefensible, and any one of them alone would already put the company in litigation暴露 territory. All three are already in writing in the company's own files.

**The exposure stack if you go ahead:**

- FMLA: lost wages **plus liquidated (double) damages**, fees, reinstatement [library/fmla_2615.md]. An 88%→ sell… let's do this cleanly: if her wages are say $NY/week, the FMLA math is roughly 2 × (back pay) + fees + reinstatement; the > double feature is automatic unless the employer shows good faith — the file below shows the opposite of good faith.
- Title VII §704(a) retaliation: back pay, front pay, compensatory damages — plus Columbia state-law parity with **longer limitations and uncapped compensatory damages** [library/columbia_at_will_exceptions.md].
- A failed retaliation defense also feeds the harassment case, because the failure to investigate destroyed the strongest *Faragher/Ellerth* shield she'd otherwise have left [library/harassment_investigation_duty.md].

---

## Why: the three problems, in calendar math

### 1. The email is the smoking gun (FMLA interference is *direct evidence*)

Timeline.md records that Tom Hale emailed you on **2026-10-02**: *"Let's get this done before she's out on leave. Once she's on FMLA it's a nightmare to move on her."* That email came **2 days after** her leave request (2026-09-30) and **4 days before** this termination request.

The library file [library/fmla_2615.md] states three things that together do the legal work:

- Terminating an employee **to prevent her from taking approved or requested leave is interference** (§2615(a)(1)); an employer may not use "the taking of FMLA leave as a negative factor" (§825.220(c)).
- "An employee who requested leave **need not have begun it**" — her request alone triggered protection.
- It is unlawful to retaliate (a)(2) for exercising or attempting to exercise FMLA rights.

Hale's email says the quiet part in writing: the objective is to move on her **before** the leave starts. That is the definition of interference in the library. Compare the dates:

| Event | Date | Gap to today |
|---|---|---|
| Harassment complaint (written, to HR) | 2026-09-12 | **24 days** |
| FMLA request | 2026-09-30 | 6 days |
| Certification submitted | 2026-10-03 | 3 days |
| Hale's "before she's out on leave" email | 2026-10-02 | 4 days |
| Termination wanted | 2026-10-06 | today |

### 2. The retaliation chronology works

Her first-ever performance document — the PIP — was opened **on 2026-09-16, four days after** her harassment complaint, by **Tom Hale himself — the accused**. The library [library/title_vii_704a.md] confirms the causation mechanics:

- "days to a few weeks" of proximity is enough; 24 days qualifies;
- pretext includes "shifting or thin justifications, disparate treatment of comparators who did not complain"; and
- decision-maker statements linking the action to protected activity are direct evidence.

Her file does not support the justification: quota attainment trended gradually (118% → 101% → 96% → 92% → 88% YTD Q1–Q3, a −30-point slide over four years, rated "Meets" every year since 2023) and there was **no prior discipline of any kind** until the accused PIP'd her [personnel file]. The PIP is only at day 20 of 60 (it would end **2026-11-15**; 40 days remain). Nobody can say she failed it.

### 3. The comparators show this is not a performance program

From `comparator_data.csv`, same role, 2026 YTD attainment:

| Employee | Age | Sex | YTD | PIP? | Complaint? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Whitcomb, D. | 42 | F | **88%** | **Yes (9/16)** | **Yes (9/12)** |
| Brennan, K. | 35 | M | 79% | No | No |
| Osei, J. | 29 | M | 84% | No | No |
| Lind, S. | 47 | F | 103% | No | No |
| Park, T. | 31 | M | 86% | No | No |

Arithmetic (shown): peer mean (79+84+103+86)/4 = 352/4 = **88.0%** — exactly Dana's number (also the five-person mean: (88+79+84+103+86)/5 = 440/5 = 88.0%). Dana clear 2–9 points **above** three younger male peers; every employee in the below-90% band other than Dana has no PIP, no termination plan. The only employee on a PIP, and the only one headed out the door, is the woman who complained. Under [library/title_vii_704a.md], that is "disparate treatment of comparators who did not complain" — textbook pretext.

*(Same pattern raises an age lens — three of four peers are younger and all three perform worse — but the library's ADEA file covers only waiver mechanics, not the substantive age-claim elements; that assessment is flagged **unverified** in risk_assessment.json.)*

---

## What to do about the harassment complaint

1. **Open an investigation immediately.** The library [library/harassment_investigation_duty.md] requires a prompt, impartial investigation with corrective action once a complaint lands. Your inbox shows it landed **2026-09-12** and got "Tom is on the road; will circle back." Twenty-four days later, nothing.
2. **Staff it outside Tom Hale's chain of command.** The library says so explicitly — and here the conflict is worse than proximity: Hale is the accused *and* the PIP author *and* appears to be advocating termination. HR cannot run a credible investigation of the same person deciding Dana's fate.
3. **Preserve everything now.** Once litigation is reasonably anticipated — an internal discrimination complaint followed by a contemplated termination qualifies — documents, ESI, and executives' emails and texts must be preserved; non-preservation risks adverse-inference instructions or sanctions [library/litigation_hold.md]. That includes Hale's 10-02 email, texts, and the acknowledgment trail from 9/12.

## What to do about the FMLA request

1. **Answer it, in writing, now.** She requested leave 2026-09-30 and its certification was submitted 10-03. HR has not responded. Silence reads as denial and hands her an interference claim on top of the email.
2. **Process the eligibility and certification determination on the merits** and, if she qualifies, approve the leave. Using "the taking of FMLA leave as a negative factor," or terminating to beat the leave to the door, is interference per §825.220(c) and she need not have begun leave [library/fmla_2615.md]. *(Note: the library states the eligibility barypress via these prohibitions but does not include the eligibility criteria themselves — e.g., service/hours thresholds — so this advice does not opine on whether she is eligible; that determination is HR's and is an open item, QUESTIONS-5.)*
3. Whatever the ultimate performance merits, **separate the time streams**: decide performance after the leave request is resolved and the investigation is done — not before, not overlapping, not "before she's out."

## About the PIP and the VP's timeline

Tell the VP the following plainly: the 60-day PIP runs until **2026-11-15** and is only 20/60 days old, so no failure has yet been established; the kickoff of "get it done this week" happens to be 24 days after she complained and 6 days after she asked for leave; and the deciding push sits in an email dated **2026-10-02** that is already discoverable and now subject to a preservation duty [library/litigation_hold.md]. If the need to move "this week" predates all that, say so and document it; on the current record it reads as motive.

## If performance still warrants action later

Only after (a) an independent decision-maker is named, (b) the investigation and FMLA determination are complete, and (c) the same discipline would justify moving on employees at 79–86% who were left alone — that is, a consistent, comparator-tested standard: let the PIP run to its own finish line, contemporaneous documentation, and a gap between protected activity and any adverse act. Anything less will read as the retaliation it already looks like [library/title_vii_704a.md].

## The separation agreement you sent: do not use it

Summarized defect list (detail in `corrected_separation_agreement_terms.md`):

- ¶7: **7 days to consider** — fails §626(f)(1)(F) (must be ≥21, or 45 in group programs) [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md]
- ¶7: **3-day revocation** — fails §626(f)(1)(G) (must be ≥7 days, and not effective until it expires) [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md]
- ¶4: releases **all claims with no future-claims carve-out** — fails §626(f)(1)(C) [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md]
- **No written advice to consult an attorney** in the excerpt — fails §626(f)(1)(E) [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md]
- ¶3 considers 4 weeks' base pay only if it is *additional* to entitlements she already has — unverifiable on this record (QUESTIONS-2) [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md]

Even a fully cured agreement is worth limited comfort here: if a release fails the OWBPA test, she can **keep the money and still sue** (*Oubre v. Entergy* [library/adea_owbpa_626f.md]), and no she-signs-first maneuver waives the claims that arose this morning.

## Retro-what to send us (QUESTIONS.md)

The answers to QUESTIONS.md (seven items) will close the residual assumptions: the full agreement text, any severance policy, decision-maker identity, investigation records, FMLA-status, comparator documentation, and pay/bonus figures for exposure quotes.

---

*Unverified-flagged items are identified inside risk_assessment.json and corrected_separation_agreement_terms.md. The recommendation — do not terminate today — does not depend on any of them.*
